brand.verdict: The no-through-gutter claim is true and verifiable, and it buys nothing: six panes at six sizes with 2-cell gaps is grey churn in a browser tab, and because nothing aligns with anything there is no rule for the eye to catch being broken. Deliberate and sloppy are indistinguishable here.

pixel.verdict: The no-through-gutter claim is true — I checked every row and column — and that is the one structurally anti-toolbar property in the whole axis. It is bought with three shapes at the 2-cell floor (2x5, 2x3, 8x2) which at 12px are already fragments; with six objects and no alignment anywhere, there is no rule for the eye to catch being broken.

user.verdict: The no-through-gutter argument is the best anti-toolbar logic in the set, but six panes with 2px gaps are grey noise in a browser tab, and with nothing aligned there is no visible rule — it reads sloppy, not lived-in.

variants.title: Glide step
variants.thesis: The system is glide reflection: one motif, one operation, applied once. The motif is a 4x6 tall pane with a 6x2 bar floating off its upper-right shoulder; the operation is translate down eight rows and mirror across the vertical axis. Crucially the bar sits high in the motif rather than at its middle, which is what stops the figure collapsing into a point rotation — I checked, and 180-degree rotation does not map this onto itself. The glide is the only symmetry it has, so the mark reads as motion rather than balance.
variants.at16: The 4x6 panes and 6x2 bars all clear the 2px floor, and the 4-cell gutters are the most generous of the six so nothing merges. The flip is carried by the left/right swap of the whole motif, which survives; what does not survive is the precise 1-row height at which the bar sits, and that does not matter because it only had to break the rotation, not be seen.
variants.risk: With only two copies, a glide is nearly indistinguishable from 'drew it twice and flipped one', which is fatal on my axis — the question is which system reads as designed fastest to someone not looking, and this one reads slowest. It also carries the least ink of the six (72 cells, 28% coverage), so at 16px it is four small blocks floating in a lot of air, and floating blocks in a browser tab read as debris rather than a mark.
variants.geometry: 72 ink cells (60 ink + 12 accent = 16.7%); COM (7.17, 7.50), off centre by 0.33 vertically, exact horizontally; symmetry: glide reflection only (verified that C2, C4, both mirrors and transpose all fail); thinnest stroke 2 cells (the 6x2 bars); gutters 2 cells (rows 7-8) and 4 cells (cols 5-8 upper, cols 7-10 lower).

brand.verdict: At 28% ink this is four rectangles floating in air, and the render confirms the author's own fear: it reads as debris, not a mark. The glide is invisible to anyone not told about it, and a 6x2 accent bar floating off a pane's shoulder means nothing at all.
brand.claimError: The reported COM pair is transposed: the actual centre of mass is (7.50, 7.17), not (7.17, 7.50). The prose ('off 0.33 vertically, exact horizontally') is correct, so the error is in the ordered pair only.

pixel.claimError: The COM tuple is transposed. Measured (7.50,7.17): exact in x, 0.33 high in y. The stated tuple (7.17,7.50) says the opposite, though the prose after it is right.
pixel.verdict: The glide is real — translate 8 down, mirror in x, and motif one lands exactly on motif two, verified. At 28% ink and four small blocks with 3-4 cell voids between them there is no silhouette at all: in a browser tab this is debris, not a mark, and the 6x2 bars are at the 2-cell floor.

user.verdict: Four small blocks floating in 72 cells of air read as debris in a browser tab, and a glide reflection with only two copies is indistinguishable from 'drew it twice and flipped one' — the author says so and is right.
user.claimError: COM tuple has its axes swapped: stated (7.17, 7.50); the grid's actual COM is (7.50, 7.17) — x exact, y off 0.33 — so the tuple contradicts the author's own prose in the (x,y) convention the rest of the set uses.

variants.title: Negative-space t
variants.thesis: The ink is two full-height columns and the 2-cell channel between them is not a divider, it is the stem of a lowercase t. A 2-row crossbar slot at rows 5-6 cuts cols 3-12, and at rows 12-13 the channel kicks 3 cells right to form the foot. The top bar at rows 0-1 caps the stem so the channel reads as a letter with a top rather than a full-bleed split, and the 3x2 void at top-right plus the 4x4 void at bottom-left keep the outline off square. It attacks the toolbar problem by taking the one feature every layout icon has — an aligned divider cross — and making it spell the product's initial.
variants.at16: The channel and the crossbar survive as a clean light-on-dark cut, and the 3-cell hinges at cols 0-2 and 13-15 hold at 3px. The foot's 3-cell kick is the first thing to blur, and once it goes the mark reads as a dagger or a plus rather than a t. The two corner notches stay obvious.
variants.risk: The t is only legible once you have been told it is there; most viewers will see a two-column window with a header bar and two slots, which is a layout icon with extra steps. Header bar plus two columns is also one of the most heavily used icon compositions in existence, so this is the variant closest to the failure mode it was drawn to escape.
variants.geometry: ink 184 cells (accent 12, 6.5%); centre of mass (7.73, 7.07) = +0.23 / -0.43 from (7.5,7.5); no symmetry axis; thinnest stroke 2 cells (top bar height, stem channel walls); gutters: stem channel 2 wide, crossbar 2 tall, foot 2 tall, corner voids 3x2 and 4x4.

brand.verdict: The render is decisive: what you see is a white cross cut out of a dark square — a first-aid or add glyph, and in dark mode a black cross on white, which is worse. It escapes the layout icon by landing on the one form the seed's own thesis names as the stock-icon tell, an aligned divider cross.
brand.claimError: The 'foot' does not function as described. The channel widens to cols 7-11 at rows 12-13 but narrows back to cols 7-8 at rows 14-15, so the stem runs past the kick all the way to the bottom edge — the negative shape is a cross with a lump on one side, not a t with a terminating foot.

pixel.claimError: The channel does not 'kick 3 cells right to form the foot'. It bulges right for two rows (cols 7-11, rows 12-13) and then returns to cols 7-8 for rows 14-15, so the negative stem runs straight off the bottom edge with a rectangular blister on its side. There is no foot, and without one the negative shape is a dagger or a plus, not a t.
pixel.verdict: At 71.9% ink with one connected region, the silhouette is the full 16x16 square minus a 3x2 and a 4x4 corner — the closest of all 36 to the plain filled square the brief bans. My 12px render reads as a header bar over two columns with two slots, which is the failure mode it was drawn to escape.

user.verdict: Nobody will find the t without the caption — the white channel reads as a divider cross in a dark slab, i.e. the toolbar icon with extra steps — and the red stub at bottom-left is never assigned a meaning by its own author: pure decoration, which the brief forbids.

variants.title: Centred master
variants.thesis: Six panes in the centredmaster arrangement: a 6x14 master running the full height down the middle, flanked by two 2-wide columns — two windows on the left, three on the right. The asymmetric window counts mean the left and right splits never line up, so the seed's misalignment idea survives while the composition becomes symmetric in mass and asymmetric in rhythm. The left column stops three rows short at the bottom, cutting a notch that keeps the outline off square; the accent is the second right-hand window, the one that is focused.
variants.at16: The master reads immediately as one dominant window; the flanking 2px columns read as "there is stuff either side" rather than as five distinct panes — the individual side windows merge into dashed rails. That is an acceptable loss: the master-plus-rails silhouette is what carries at this size.
variants.risk: Two-cell columns are the absolute legal minimum and at 16px they read as a border, which flips the whole mark from "three columns of windows" to "a framed document" — the exact opposite of a terminal. It is also the most nearly symmetric variant, which edges toward the centred-everything look the client rejects.
variants.geometry: 122 ink cells (8 accent, 6.6%); COM (7.60, 7.26) → off (+0.10, -0.24); near mirror-symmetric in mass, asymmetric in split positions; thinnest stroke 2 cells (side columns); all gutters 2 (cols 3-4 and 11-12; rows 6-7 left, rows 4-5 and 10-11 right).

brand.verdict: The 2-cell flanking columns do exactly what was feared — at 16px they read as a hatched border, flipping the mark from three columns of windows to a framed document with margin rules. Near-symmetric mass plus a 6-cell centre slab is the centred-everything look the client rejects.

pixel.verdict: Five of the six panes are 2 cells wide — the absolute floor — and my 12px downsample confirms they render as a row of dim ':@:' ticks, i.e. a picket fence, not windows. Symmetric mass with a master down the middle is the framed-document read the brief is trying to kill, and the 2x4 accent is a 2px-wide sliver.

user.verdict: At 16px the 2-wide side columns compress into a border and the whole mark flips to 'framed document' — the author names this failure in their own risk statement and ships it anyway.

variants.title: Module-locked asymmetry
variants.thesis: No symmetry at all. The discipline is a strict 3x3 module grid — 3-cell modules at cols 1-3 / 6-8 / 11-13 and rows 1-3 / 6-8 / 11-13, with 2-cell gutters — plus one rule: every pane is an integer number of modules and every pane edge lands on a module line. Five panes span one or two modules each and no two are the same shape; the top-left module is left empty so the composition cannot close into a rectangle. Deliberateness is proved by alignment rather than reflection: nothing is centred, and yet nothing sits anywhere but on the grid.
variants.at16: 3-cell panes and 2-cell gutters both survive, but with no margin for error — the mark reduces to three 3px columns with a 3px bar over the right two. The empty top-left module is a 3x3 bite and stays visible, and it is the only thing keeping the silhouette off a rectangle. This is the most fragile of the six at favicon size.
variants.risk: Three columns under a header bar is very close to what a stock 'layout' toolbar icon actually looks like, so this is the cut most likely to lose the argument to the harsh critic outright — vacating one corner module is a thin defence. It also carries the least ink weight at the smallest stroke, so in a dark tab it will look grey and spindly next to the other five.
variants.geometry: 90 ink cells (81 ink + 9 accent = 10.0%); COM (7.50, 7.67), off centre by 0.00 and 0.17; symmetry: none (C1); underlying system is a 3x3 modular grid, 3-cell module + 2-cell gutter, all edges module-locked; thinnest stroke 3 cells; gutters exactly 2 cells (cols 4-5, cols 9-10, rows 4-5, rows 9-10).

brand.verdict: Three columns under a header bar is not near a stock layout icon, it is one, and at 35% ink with 3-cell strokes it is also the most spindly thing here — in dark mode it goes grey and thin next to everything else. Vacating one corner module is not a silhouette.
brand.claimError: 'no two are the same shape' is false: the left and right panes are both 3x8, and the accent and lower-centre panes are both 3x3 — two congruent pairs out of five panes. The reported COM pair is also transposed (actual (7.67, 7.50), so the 0.17 offset is in x, not y).

pixel.claimError: Two errors. 'No two [panes] are the same shape' is false — the left and right panes are both 3x8 and the accent and bottom-centre pane are both 3x3. And the COM tuple is transposed: measured (7.67,7.50), off (+0.17, 0.00). Unstated: the mark's bbox is cols 1-13 / rows 1-13, so it carries a 1-cell margin top and left against a 2-cell margin right and bottom.
pixel.verdict: Min stroke 3 and 35% ink means it holds at 16px but renders spindly and, because of the uneven margin, visibly parked up and left inside its own tile. Three columns under a header bar with one corner vacated is the stock layout icon with a corner vacated.

user.verdict: Three thin columns under a header bar is the stock layout icon drawn lighter, and at 90 cells it will sit grey and spindly next to every other mark on the page.
user.claimError: 'No two panes are the same shape' is false: the left and right columns are both exactly 3x8, and the accent and bottom-centre blocks are both exactly 3x3. COM is also swapped: actual (7.67, 7.50) — off 0.17 horizontally, not vertically as the stated (7.50, 7.67) implies.

critiques.overall: Every grid is technically clean — 36/36 are valid 16x16 with no 1-cell stroke and no 1-cell interior gutter anywhere — and that is the problem: rendered at literal 16px in a row, roughly thirty of them are the same tile, a dark square with white slots, and the six axes explored (offset amount, pane count, symmetry group, ink weight, focus device, concept push) almost all vary things that are invisible at favicon size. The strongest cluster is the three marks that stop drawing filled rectangles inside a bounding square at all: weight-gutter-inverted, which inverts figure and ground so there is no outer rectangle left to mistake for a toolbar button; sym-transpose-bracket, which abandons the box for two interlocking L's; and push-cascade, which goes light and stepped. Each of those wins by leaving the brief — one drops the panes, one drops the panes and the accent, one depicts cascading rather than tiling — which is itself the finding: within this territory, faithfulness to the seed and escape from the generic read are in direct opposition. The second recurring failure is the accent: it is repeatedly a 4-6 cell speck (count-pair-cursor, sym-pinwheel-void, focus-block-cursor) that dies in dark mode, or a corner block (offset-master-stack, offset-pinwheel-slabs, sym-point-rotation) that decorates instead of meaning, and in six marks stripping it collapses the whole idea. What the set is still missing is the obvious middle: a mark that keeps solid panes and gutters but removes 25-40% of the bounding square as one large void — weight-subtract-void and push-cursor-pane are the only two that even gesture at it, both at half strength — and a version of the gutter-inversion move that has somewhere honest for the vermilion to live.

Credit first: not one of the 36 breaks the hard rules. I measured every horizontal and vertical run in all 36 grids and there is no 1-cell stroke and no 1-cell gap anywhere; the minimum interior gap is 2 in every mark except sym-glide-step (3) and sym-transpose-bracket (8). The failures are all one level up. The dominant recurring fault is that the differentiating feature is at the 2-cell floor while the bulk of the mark sits at 6-9 cells: hollow interiors that my bloom test closes (weight-hollow-frames loses 16 hole-cells at mild bloom, focus-solid-among-outlines' 3x3 hole collapses to one cell), a 1-cell overhang carrying focus-floating-pane's whole concept, and 2-cell rails and cursors carrying count-pair-cursor, focus-edge-rail and sym-nautilus. The second recurring fault nobody in the set tested for: accents parked in corners, where an avatar circle crop removes 39-75% of them (push-crop-bleed 75%, push-t-panes 62%, weight-crop-bleed and push-cursor-pane 56%, weight-focus-solid 55%, focus-title-strip 50%, offset-master-stack 48%) — and, related, nobody checked light-mode luminance contrast for accents that abut or are enclosed by near-black ink, which is why count-pair-cursor, push-cascade and focus-block-cursor all have accents that will read in dark mode and smudge in light. The strongest cluster is the four marks that stop trying to be a tiled rectangle and commit to a shape with a hole or a step in it — sym-transpose-bracket and push-cascade at the top, then weight-gutter-inverted and weight-subtract-void, which are also the only marks whose silhouette event is 5 cells or larger and therefore the only ones that still exist at 12px. What the set is still missing is a mark that keeps the legible four-pane tiling read and has a silhouette event big enough to survive: over half of these are a full-bleed rectangle whose only outline incident is a 2-4 cell corner bite, which is rule 5 in spirit even where it passes on the letter.

The strongest cluster is the marks that add a second, terminal-specific object to the tiling instead of just rearranging tiles — offset-master-stack and offset-half-brick-bond (product-true layouts that stay legible), push-t-panes and push-cursor-pane (a block cursor doing the 'this is a shell' work) — plus two escape hatches, sym-transpose-bracket and weight-gutter-inverted, which are the best pure logos in the set but only by leaving the solid-pane territory. The recurring failure is that stagger alone does not survive 16px: a dozen variants are rectangles-with-offset-gutters whose differences evaporate in a browser tab, at which point they regress to exactly the toolbar icon the client is paying to escape; the second recurring failure is accents sliding to corners and edges where they decorate instead of meaning focus. Notably, several authors' own risk statements are the correct final verdict on their marks (centred-master, title-strip, cell-baseline, cascade), and the symmetry-axis author got their own COM geometry backwards three times. What the set still lacks is the obvious synthesis: a master-and-stack composition of solid panes with an ink-drawn, monochrome-safe block cursor anchoring scale — offset-master-stack's body with push-cursor-pane's idea drawn in ink would beat everything scored here.

synth.intro: Twenty-five candidate territories went out and one came back. frame-tiling-misaligned is four solid panes on a single vertical gutter whose horizontal splits deliberately do not line up. The client picked it because a tiling window manager is what this product's audience looks at all day, and because the framework's own layout engine tiles panes. The mark is a picture of the thing. It also carries one problem, and every variant here is an attempt on it: a tiled rectangle is the layout button in every design tool's toolbar. Six agents attacked from six directions: how far the dividers can miss, how many panes there are, which symmetry group generates them, how much ink they carry, how focus gets stated, and what happens when the territory is abandoned. That produced 36 grids. Three critics scored all of them, a brand director, a pixel technician measuring bloom and crop behaviour, and a developer who runs a tiling WM. Where they disagreed, it is noted.

axisNotes.note: The question was how badly the dividers can miss. Answers ran from a 2-cell stagger to an 8-cell teleport, and both ends failed. interlock-pair (4.0) is a quartered square with a wobble in the seam, and jogged-gutter reaches 72% ink, a filled square with a crack in it. The middle held: master-stack (6.2) pushes the offset until no two edges share a line.

Two panes up to six. The finding is that pane count does not fix genre. Six panes are grey churn in a browser tab (dense-six, 3.5), three equal columns are the oldest toolbar glyph there is (thirds-ragged, 3.8), and two panes plus a cursor collapse into a split-view toggle in monochrome. The best idea, a status bar with a workspace tag, arrived inside a browser-window frame. Weakest axis in the set.

Which symmetry group reads as designed fastest. This axis produced both the highest-scoring mark (transpose-bracket, 7.5) and the lowest (module-lock, 3.0). The lesson is that the more famous the group, the more anticipated the result: verified C4 renders as a loading spinner, and a glide with only two copies reads as drew-it-twice-and-flipped-one. Transpose won because no logo genre owns it yet.

Coverage from 28% to 70%. One finding here is genuinely useful and was measured rather than asserted: subtraction beats hollowing. A 5x5 missing quadrant survives everything, while a 2x2 hole shuts completely under mild bloom and 3-cell walls pinch to slots. The heavy end confirmed the accusation exactly, full-bleed-bite being the layout tile with one corner chipped off. The light end produced gutter-inverted.

How a flat 16px drawing says which pane is focused. All six devices failed, each in its own way. A title bar is the chrome tiling WMs exist to delete, the edge rail measures identical to the gutter beside it, the block cursor butts the frame wall, and the floating pane's overhang is 1 cell, under the brief's own floor. Top score 5.3. Accent placement is unsolved.

Permission to leave the territory, which bought the highest ceiling and the widest disagreement. cascade is the second most robust drawing in the set and depicts the opposite of tiling. t-panes says two true things at once and duplicates the mark the client already has. cell-baseline is a good 400px sticker whose entire concept is gone at 16px, which its own author states.

finalists.case: Highest mean in the set at 7.5, and the only mark all three lenses placed near the top. Two unequal 3-thick L-brackets around a verified clean 8x8 void, the largest interior gap here by a factor of nearly three. Two cells close under bloom, six are lost to a circle crop, and with no accent the favicon, the sticker and the monochrome stamp are one drawing.
finalists.against: It has left the territory. There are no panes in it, and interlocking L-brackets are a crowded genre of their own: crop marks, focus reticles, the macOS fullscreen control. The transpose invariance is a real product metaphor that no viewer will ever see.

finalists.case: The only structural answer to the stated problem. Delete the panes and draw the divider system instead: a 3-cell spine with one arm running left and one running right, four rows apart. 34% ink, one connected region, no interior detail to lose, three cells clipped by a circle crop. It reads as a box-drawing glyph, which is the most terminal-native form anyone produced.
finalists.against: Cold, it can read as a pipe fitting or a mis-drawn H. Having removed the panes there is nowhere honest for the accent, so the mark cannot say which window is focused, and that is the signal the rest of the set spends itself on.

finalists.case: The one variant the developer lens called a picture of an actual dwm screen rather than an icon of one, scoring 7.5 there. A 9x11 master beside a slotted 5-wide stack, with a verified 2-cell minimum clearance between every master edge and every stack edge, so no line can be read as a near miss. Three objects, min run 5, nothing in it can fail at 16px.
finalists.against: The brand lens gave it 5: wide block left, slotted bar right, coloured rectangle in the top-right corner is the page-with-right-rail wireframe. The accent parks in a corner, and 12 of its 25 cells fall outside an avatar circle crop.

finalists.case: By measurement the strongest drawing after the brackets. COM lands exactly on (7.50, 7.50), the monochrome silhouette has exact C2 broken only by the accent, the step is a uniform +3, the bands a uniform 4 rows, every gutter is 2, nothing closes under bloom, and it still reads at 12px. Three masses running off opposite edges give it a staircase outline no filled tile can imitate.
finalists.against: It draws cascading windows, which is the Windows 3.1 toolbar button and the opposite of what the layout engine does, so the better it renders the more wrong it is about the product. The 2-cell accent butts the bar it belongs to and vanishes in mono.

synth.recommendation: Take weight-gutter-inverted. It is the only variant that removes the bounding rectangle rather than nibbling at it, so the toolbar-button reading has nothing left to attach to. At 34% ink, 3-cell strokes and one connected region it is tied with the brackets for the safest thing here at 16px, and with no accent the tab icon, the sticker and the mono stamp are the same drawing. It does not beat the current mark, and the page should say so. baseline-a-refined names the product and says shell in one move, with the block cursor sitting on the foot of the t. This one says tiling and does not say terminaltui. Run it as the app and tab mark beside the wordmark rather than as a replacement. If a standalone object is wanted instead, take sym-transpose-bracket and accept the genre risk. Do not take push-t-panes: it is the incumbent's own idea drawn worse, and 1.17 cells off centre.
synth.disagreements: The widest split is push-t-panes: brand 3, pixel 5, user 7. The developer saw a shell prompt, a pixel t with a block cursor parked at the baseline. The brand director saw a plus sign with a loose red square and measured COM 1.17 cells low-right. offset-master-stack splits the same way, brand 5 against user 7.5, and offset-half-brick-bond and sym-pinwheel-void repeat the pattern. It is consistent: the developer rewards product truth that the brand director reads as genre collision, while the pixel technician sits between them and scores only what survives a downscale. Marks that need domain knowledge score high on one lens and low on another.
